claim: The ancestral population (A6140) was domesticated to constant low salt conditions (25 mM NaCl) for 140 generations.
source: The ancestral population for experimental evolution (A6140) was ultimately derived from a hybrid population of 16 isolates and domestication to a standard laboratory environment in low salt (25 mM NaCl) growth-media conditions for 140 generations (Teotonio et al., 2012; Noble et al., 2017).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: GA[1,2,4] replicate populations were exposed to a gradual increase in salt concentration (8 mM increase each generation) for 35 generations.
source: GA[1,2,4] replicate populations were derived from A6140, with limited founder effects, and independently exposed for 35 generations to a gradual change in salt concentration (8 mM increase each generation) and then kept in constant high salt (305 mM NaCl) for 15 generations.
evidence: Explicitly described in the experimental design section of Results.

claim: Replicate populations were maintained at high population sizes (N=10^4) during experimental evolution.
source: During the experiment, replicate populations were maintained at high population sizes (N=104), and from generation 35 onwards, hermaphrodite self-fertilization became predominant (Theologidis et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in the experimental design section with citation.

claim: Hermaphrodite self-fertilization became predominant from generation 35 onwards.
source: During the experiment, replicate populations were maintained at high population sizes (N=104), and from generation 35 onwards, hermaphrodite self-fertilization became predominant (Theologidis et al., 2014).
evidence: Explicitly stated with supporting citation.

claim: Effective population sizes have been estimated at Ne=10^3 in the domestication low salt environment under partial selfing.
source: Using genomic data, effective population sizes have been estimated at Ne=103 in the domestication low salt environment and under partial selfing (Chelo and Teotónio, 2013).
evidence: Stated with citation to genomic analysis.

claim: Locomotion behavior is defined by six traits: the transition rates between stillness, forward movement, and backward movement.
source: Six traits defined locomotion behavior: the transition rates between movement states, stillness, forward, and backward (Mallard et al., 2022).
evidence: Explicitly defined in the experimental design section with citation.

claim: There is extensive phenotypic plasticity for locomotion behavior traits and body size between low and high salt environments in the ancestral population.
source: We find extensive phenotypic plasticity for locomotion behavior traits and body size (Figure 1, Table 2).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to figure and table showing data.

claim: Most transition rates are plastic with salt, except from forward to backward movement states.
source: Most transition rates are plastic with salt, except from forward to backward movement states.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Results section describing phenotypic plasticity.

claim: Body size shrinks in high salt as expected.
source: As expected, body size shrinks in high salt.
evidence: Stated as an observation consistent with expectations.

claim: Osmotic pressure from high salt concentration in the growth media shrinks individual body size because of water cell loss.
source: Osmotic pressure from high salt concentration in the growth media shrinks individual body size because of water cell loss (Urso and Lamitina, 2021).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation to mechanistic study.

claim: High salt lowers embryo to adult survival and retards growth until maturity in the ancestral population under laboratory conditions.
source: For the ancestral population, and in our laboratory conditions, high salt also lowers embryo to adult survival and retards growth until maturity (Theologidis et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citation to previous work on the same population.

claim: Body size has the same sign as the transition rates from still and from forward to backward (SB and FB) and the opposite sign relative to the other transition rates in δp.
source: Body size has the same sign of the transition rates from still and from forward to backward (SB and FB) and the opposite sign relative to the other transition rates.
evidence: Stated in Results describing the phenotypic plasticity canonical trait.

claim: There is significant genetic variance for all transition rates and body size in high and low salt environments, except for the transition rate from backward to still in low salt.
source: We find significant genetic variance for all transition rates and body size, in high and low salt environments, except for the transition rate from backward to still in low salt (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figures showing genetic variance estimates.

claim: The G-matrix size is similar between high and low salt environments.
source: The G-matrix size is similar between environments (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing total genetic variance.

claim: In both high and low salt environments, transition rates from still to forward or to backward (SF or SB) are negatively correlated with the other transition rates and positively correlated with each other.
source: In both high and low salt environments, transition rates from still to forward or to backward (SF or SB) are negatively correlated with the other transition rates and positively correlated with each other.
evidence: Stated in Results describing genetic covariances.

claim: Body size shows positive genetic covariances with SF and SB.
source: Body size shows positive genetic covariances with SF and SB.
evidence: Stated in Results describing genetic covariances.

claim: The next two canonical traits contain less genetic variation (between 6% and 20%) but are larger than null expectations.
source: The next two canonical traits contain less genetic variation (between 6% and 20%) but are larger than null expectations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure comparing to null distributions.

claim: Only the first two canonical traits of the G-matrix have similar trait loadings between high and low salt environments.
source: Only the first two canonical traits of the G-matrix have a similar trait loadings between environments (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to source data.

claim: Phenotypic plasticity is not aligned with the ancestral G-matrix in high salt.
source: Phenotypic plasticity is not aligned with the G-matrix (Figure 3).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing alignment analysis.

claim: There is genetic variance for self-fertility in high salt in the ancestral population.
source: We find genetic variance for self-fertility in high salt (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing genetic variance estimates.

claim: The transition rates from still to forward or from still to backward (SF or SB) measured in high salt have positive genetic covariances with self-fertility.
source: We also find that the transition rates from still to forward or from still to backward (SF or SB) measured in high salt have positive genetic covariances with self-fertility, and all other transition rates have negative covariances (Figure 4).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing genetic covariances with fitness.

claim: Small or no selection differentials exist in low salt transition rates.
source: Small or no selection differentials exist in low salt transition rates
evidence: Stated in Results describing selection differentials.

claim: Only body size shows a clear positive selection differential in both high and low salt environments.
source: and only body size shows a clear positive selection differential in both environments.
evidence: Stated in Results describing selection differentials.

claim: There is an increase in the mean fitness of all three replicate populations (GA[1,2,4]50) relative to the ancestral population in high salt.
source: We find an increase in the mean fitness of all three replicate populations (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing competition assay results.

claim: By generation 50, populations adapted to the high salt environment.
source: By generation 50, populations adapted to the high salt environment.
evidence: Stated as conclusion from fitness measurements.

claim: There was phenotypic divergence for locomotion traits and body size measured in high salt concomitant with adaptation.
source: Concomitant with adaptation, there was phenotypic divergence for the locomotion traits and body size measured in high salt (Figure 6, Table 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure and table showing phenotypic measurements.

claim: For each transition rate, at least one replicate GA population differed from the ancestor.
source: From the univariate models, we find that for each transition rate, at least one replicate GA population differed from the ancestor
evidence: Stated in Results describing univariate analysis.

claim: The three replicates showed significant divergence for three transition rates.
source: and that the three replicates showed significant divergence for three transition rates (Figure 6, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure and source data.

claim: For body size, only one replicate population diverged from the ancestral population in high salt.
source: For body size we find that only one replicate populations diverged from the ancestral population.
evidence: Stated in Results describing body size evolution.

claim: The amount of genetic variance did not limit phenotypic divergence, as the back-to-still and forward-to-still transition rates (BS and FS) diverged while showing the lowest genetic variances in the ancestral population.
source: The amount of genetic variance did not limit phenotypic divergence, as the back-to-still and forward-to-still transition rates (BS and FS) diverged while showing the lowest genetic variances in the ancestral population (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing ancestral genetic variances.

claim: In the low salt environment, there was less phenotypic divergence than in the high salt environment, with only three out of the six transition rates having at least two replicate populations significantly different from the ancestor.
source: In the low salt environment, there was less phenotypic divergence than in the high salt environment, with only three out of the six transition rates having at least two replicate populations significantly different from the ancestor (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure supplement.

claim: Unlike in high salt, body size in low salt showed a marked increase after experimental evolution in all replicate populations.
source: Unlike in high salt, body size in low salt showed a marked increase after experimental evolution in all replicate populations.
evidence: Stated in Results describing low salt phenotypic divergence.

claim: The size of the high salt G-matrix was reduced during experimental evolution, independently of the replicate population.
source: This analysis shows that the size of the high salt G-matrix was reduced during experimental evolution, independently of the replicate population (Figure 7, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing G-matrix evolution.

claim: Most genetic variances for the GA populations differ from null expectations.
source: However, we continue to find that most genetic variances for the GA populations differ from null expectations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure supplement comparing to null distributions.

claim: Eigendecomposition of the GA G-matrices indicates that 3–5 canonical traits differ from null expectations.
source: Eigendecomposition of the GA G-matrices indicates that 3–5 canonical traits differ from null expectations (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure supplement showing eigendecomposition.

claim: Evolved populations continued to have significant genetic variances in the three canonical traits of ancestral standing genetic variation.
source: Furthermore, evolved populations continued to have significant genetic variances in the three canonical traits of ancestral standing genetic variation (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure supplement showing projections.

claim: Random skewers analysis shows that 250 out of 1000 random phenotypic directions showed a significant difference between the ancestral and at least one of the evolved populations.
source: Random skewers analysis shows that when projecting the four high salt G-matrices along 1000 random phenotypic directions, 250 of them showed a significant difference between the ancestral and at least one of the evolved populations (see Methods).
evidence: Stated in Results describing random skewers analysis.

claim: In the emax canonical trait, at least 2 of the 3 evolved populations showed a reduction in variance.
source: In this canonical trait at least 2 of the 3 evolved populations showed a reduction in variance (Figure 7C).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing genetic variance along emax.

claim: Phenotypic selection gradients for all traits are highly heterogeneous because higher phenotypic divergence has an outsize effect on the mean and error estimates.
source: We find that phenotypic selection gradients for all traits are highly heterogeneous because higher phenotypic divergence has an outsize effect on the mean and error estimates.
evidence: Stated in Results describing selection gradient estimates.

claim: The phenotypic selection gradients overlap with the corresponding genetic selection gradients for at least one replicate population.
source: Nonetheless, the phenotypic selection gradients overlap with the corresponding genetic selection gradients for at least one replicate population (Figure 9A; Figure 9—source data 1, Figure 9—source data 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing selection gradients.

claim: Evidence for a lack of overlap between selection gradients in two replicate populations is found for the transition rate backward-to-forward and for body size.
source: Evidence for a lack of overlap between selection gradients in two replicate populations is found for the transition rate backward-to-forward and for body size.
evidence: Stated in Results describing selection gradient comparisons.

claim: Only for the transition rate SB is there an overlap of selection gradients for all three replicate populations.
source: Only for the transition rate SB is there an overlap of selection gradients for all three replicate populations.
evidence: Stated in Results describing selection gradient comparisons.

claim: For traits measured in high salt, the angle between selection differentials and observed phenotypic divergence is low for all replicates.
source: For traits measured in high salt, we find that the angle between selection differentials and observed phenotypic divergence is low for all replicates (Figure 9B).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing angle analysis.

claim: When traits are measured in low salt, expected and observed responses are not aligned.
source: In contrast, when traits are measured in low salt, expected and observed responses are not aligned.
evidence: Stated in Results comparing high and low salt predictions.

claim: For all traits measured in high salt, and across replicate populations, observed phenotypic divergence is on average 3.5 times the selection differentials.
source: For all traits measured in high salt, and across replicate populations, observed phenotypic divergence is on average, across traits and replicates, 3.5 times the selection differentials (Figure 9C).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing ratio analysis.

claim: There is evidence of direct selection on SB and backward-to-forward (BF), as well as on body size.
source: There is evidence of direct selection on SB and backward-to-forward (BF), as well as on body size (Figure 9A, Figure 9—source data 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure showing genetic selection gradients.

claim: There is a positive genetic selection gradient for SB.
source: We find a positive genetic selection gradient for SB
evidence: Stated in Results describing genetic selection gradients.

claim: There is a negative genetic selection gradient for BF.
source: and a negative genetic selection gradient for BF.
evidence: Stated in Results describing genetic selection gradients.

claim: There is a positive selection gradient for body size, opposite in sign to its association with other traits in the canonical traits of standing genetic variation, and in the canonical traits of phenotypic and genetic divergence.
source: There is also a positive selection gradient for body size, opposite in sign to its association with other traits in the canonical traits of standing genetic variation, and in the canonical traits of phenotypic and genetic divergence (Table 3).
evidence: Stated with reference to table showing canonical trait loadings.

claim: None of the genetic selection gradient estimates differ from zero when sampling both the G-matrix and the selection differentials from their respective posterior distributions to obtain credible intervals.
source: However, none of the genetic selection gradient estimates differ from zero when sampling both the G-matrix and the selection differentials from their respective posterior distributions to obtain credible intervals (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated with reference to figure supplement showing alternative analysis.

claim: The direction of adaptive multivariate phenotypic evolution can be predicted from the ancestral selection differentials, particularly when the traits were measured in the new environment.
source: We show that the direction of adaptive multivariate phenotypic evolution can be predicted from the ancestral selection differentials, particularly when the traits were measured in the new environment.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: The evolution of individual traits does not always occur in the direction of selection.
source: Interestingly, the evolution of individual traits does not always occur in the direction of selection
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: Trait responses to selection are not always homogeneous among replicate populations.
source: nor are trait responses to selection always homogeneous among replicate populations.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main finding.

claim: The phenotypic dimension with most of the ancestral standing genetic variation only partially aligns with the phenotypic dimension under directional selection.
source: These observations are explained because the phenotypic dimension with most of the ancestral standing genetic variation only partially aligns with the phenotypic dimension under directional selection.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as an explanation for the findings.

claim: The direction of multivariate adaptive phenotypic evolution is predictable for tens of generations.
source: These findings validate selection theory and suggest that the direction of multivariate adaptive phenotypic evolution is predictable for tens of generations.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion.

claim: Predicting adaptive phenotypic evolution depends on invariable selection gradients and on the stability of the genetic covariances between the component traits of the multivariate phenotype.
source: Predicting adaptive phenotypic evolution depends on invariable selection gradients and on the stability of the genetic covariances between the component traits of the multivariate phenotype.
evidence: Stated in the Abstract as a premise.

claim: Many traits in natural populations are heritable across generations and under natural selection.
source: Many traits in natural populations are heritable across generations and under natural selection (Walsh and Lynch, 2018).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation to textbook.

claim: Phenotypic evolution is often not observed or is of opposite direction than predicted, because of environmental or genetic correlations between the traits of interest with unmeasured traits.
source: Often, however, phenotypic evolution is not observed (Merilä et al., 2001; Pujol et al., 2018), or is of opposite direction than predicted, because of environmental or genetic correlations between the traits of interest with unmeasured traits (Morrissey et al., 2012; Hajduk et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations to empirical studies.

claim: Lande's equation predicts adaptive phenotypic evolution but might fail when indirect selection is important.
source: Lande's equation predicts adaptive phenotypic evolution but might fail when indirect selection is important.
evidence: Stated in Introduction as a limitation of the theory.

claim: Indirect selection results from unmeasured traits being genetically correlated with the measured traits or when there is correlated selection between measured and unmeasured traits.
source: Indirect selection results from unmeasured traits being genetically correlated with the measured traits or when there is correlated selection between measured and unmeasured traits (Lande and Arnold, 1983; Rausher, 1992).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations.

claim: Distinguishing direct from indirect selection is not possible with Robertson's STNS.
source: However, distinguishing direct from indirect selection is not possible with Robertson's STNS
evidence: Stated in Introduction as a limitation.

claim: Using Lande's equation with the genetic selection gradients to predict adaptive phenotypic evolution over several generations depends not only on invariable selection gradients but also on the stability of the G-matrix.
source: Unfortunately, using Lande's equation with the genetic selection gradients to predict adaptive phenotypic evolution over several generations depends not only on invariable selection gradients but also on the stability of the G-matrix.
evidence: Stated in Introduction as a key challenge.

claim: The G-matrix is bound to evolve in the short-term because of selection.
source: In addition, the G-matrix is bound to evolve in the short-term because of selection (Cheverud, 1996; Barton and Turelli, 1987; Turelli, 1988; Shaw et al., 1995)
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations to theoretical work.

claim: There is mixed empirical evidence that the G-matrix can evolve to align with the orientations of selection.
source: although there is mixed empirical evidence that the G-matrix can evolve to align with the orientations of selection (Steppan et al., 2002; Arnold et al., 2008; Chenoweth et al., 2010; Ramakers et al., 2018; Johansson et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations to empirical studies.

claim: The reduction in the size of the G-matrix due to drift can be predicted because it is inversely proportional to the effective population size.
source: The reduction in the size of the G-matrix due to drift can be predicted because it is inversely proportional to the effective population size (Lande, 1976; Lynch and Hill, 1986; Barton et al., 2017)
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations to theoretical work.

claim: The shape of the G-matrix will change unpredictably because all populations are finite, and bottlenecks and founder effects are common.
source: but the shape of the G-matrix will change unpredictably because all populations are finite, and bottlenecks and founder effects are common (Phillips et al., 2001; Phillips and McGuigan, 2006).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations.

claim: Drift might impact ongoing phenotypic evolution long before the mutation-selection balance is reached.
source: Hence, besides selection, drift might also impact ongoing phenotypic evolution long before the mutation-selection balance is reached (Whitlock et al., 2002; Mallard et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations.

claim: The ancestral population contains abundant but neutral standing genetic variation for locomotion behavior.
source: Our ancestral population was domesticated to constant low salt conditions for 140 generations and contains abundant but neutral standing genetic variation for locomotion behavior (Mallard et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation to previous work.

claim: The experimental regime exacerbates drift and inbreeding because of a slow rate of environmental change until reaching the target high salt environment.
source: Although replicate populations were maintained at high population sizes, our experimental regime exacerbates drift and inbreeding because of a slow rate of environmental change until reaching the target high salt environment (Guzella et al., 2018)
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation.

claim: High salt favors hermaphrodite self-fertilization.
source: and because high salt favors hermaphrodite self-fertilization (Theologidis et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation.

claim: Delayed male development results in hermaphrodites reproducing mostly by self-fertilization.
source: As hermaphrodites cannot mate with each other, delayed male development results in hermaphrodites reproducing mostly by self-fertilization.
evidence: Stated in Introduction as a logical consequence.

claim: During domestication, movement was reduced from that observed among wild isolates.
source: During domestication, movement was reduced from that observed among wild isolates (Mallard et al., 2022)
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation.

claim: Hermaphrodites can further reduce movement in high salt during experimental evolution as males become less frequent and cannot harass them.
source: and hermaphrodites can further reduce movement in high salt during experimental evolution as males become less frequent and cannot harass them (Barr et al., 2018; Cutter et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations.

claim: The canonical trait of locomotion behavior with the most mutational variance in low salt conditions differs from that with the most standing genetic variation found after domestication.
source: We further know that the canonical trait of locomotion behavior with the most mutational variance in low salt conditions differs from that with the most standing genetic variation found after domestication (Mallard et al., 2023).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation.

claim: Several studies have shown that C. elegans mutants insensitive to high salt have specific defects in backward or forward movement, in some of these mutants independently of body size effects.
source: Consistent with these observations, several studies have shown that C. elegans mutants insensitive to high salt have specific defects in backward or forward movement, in some of these mutants independently of body size effects (Fujiwara et al., 2002; Swierczek et al., 2011; Zhen and Samuel, 2015).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations to genetic studies.

claim: Movement can increase during experimental evolution due to more foraging and dwelling, as the bacterial food is not as dense in high salt.
source: On the other hand, movement can increase during experimental evolution due to more foraging and dwelling, as the bacterial food is not as dense in high salt (Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation.

claim: Foraging, dwelling and mate interactions in C. elegans can be described as a complex collection of distinct behavioral states, which vary in the duration of activity and movement direction.
source: Both foraging, dwelling and mate interactions in C. elegans can be described as a complex collection of distinct behavioral states, which vary in the duration of activity and movement direction (Flavell et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citation.

claim: Individual locomotion behavior in 1-dimensional space is mathematically defined by six traits, the six transition rates between stillness, moving forward, and moving backward.
source: For this reason, we mathematically define individual locomotion behavior in 1-dimensional space by six traits, the six transition rates between stillness, moving forward, and moving backward (Mallard et al., 2022, Mallard et al., 2023).
evidence: Stated in Introduction with citations.

claim: Ancestral phenotypic plasticity can be considered 'non-adaptive'.
source: Ancestral phenotypic plasticity can thus be considered 'non-adaptive' (Ghalambor et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with citation.

claim: Body size evolution in low salt supports the hypothesis that phenotypic plasticity facilitated the evolution of novelty.
source: In other words, body size evolution in low salt supports the long-held hypothesis that phenotypic plasticity facilitated the evolution of novelty (Wagner and Lynch, 2010; Moczek et al., 2011; Levis et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with citations.

claim: Using Lande's equation with genetic selection gradients is valid to predict the direction of phenotypic evolution in a new environment, after a gradual environmental change for 35 generations and 15 generations in the new environment.
source: In sum, we have shown that using Lande's equation with genetic selection gradients is valid to predict the direction of phenotypic evolution in a new environment, after a gradual environmental change for 35 generations and 15 generations in the new environment.
evidence: Stated in Discussion as a main conclusion.

claim: Selection theory does not necessarily predict the direction or magnitude of evolutionary change in all the component traits of the multivariate phenotype, especially if the traits are not measured in the new environment.
source: However, selection theory not necessarily predict the direction or magnitude of evolutionary change in all the component traits of the multivariate phenotype, especially if the traits are not measured in the new environment.
evidence: Stated in Discussion as a main conclusion.

claim: There are variable and complex genetic and environmental dependencies between individual traits.
source: This is because there are variable and complex genetic and environmental dependencies between individual traits.
evidence: Stated in Discussion as an explanation.

claim: 186 inbred lines were derived from the ancestral population A6140.
source: (186, 61, 61, and 42 lines from the ancestral and evolved populations, respectively, with most lines being phenotyped twice; see Methods for details).
evidence: Stated in Results describing experimental design.

claim: 61 inbred lines were derived from GA150.
source: (186, 61, 61, and 42 lines from the ancestral and evolved populations, respectively, with most lines being phenotyped twice; see Methods for details).
evidence: Stated in Results describing experimental design.

claim: 61 inbred lines were derived from GA250.
source: (186, 61, 61, and 42 lines from the ancestral and evolved populations, respectively, with most lines being phenotyped twice; see Methods for details).
evidence: Stated in Results describing experimental design.

claim: 42 inbred lines were derived from GA450.
source: (186, 61, 61, and 42 lines from the ancestral and evolved populations, respectively, with most lines being phenotyped twice; see Methods for details).
evidence: Stated in Results describing experimental design.

claim: Most inbred lines were phenotyped twice.
source: (186, 61, 61, and 42 lines from the ancestral and evolved populations, respectively, with most lines being phenotyped twice; see Methods for details).
evidence: Stated in Results describing experimental design.

claim: Assuming an infinitesimal model of trait inheritance, drift is expected to lead to a loss of genetic variance by (1-1/2Ne) at each generation.
source: Assuming an infinitesimal model of trait inheritance, drift is expected to lead to a loss of genetic variance by (1-1/2Ne) at each generation (Barton et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with citation to theory.

claim: Even in the unrealistic situation of complete selfing during the experiment, and considering effective population sizes on the order of 1000, less than 5% of genetic variance was expected to be lost by genetic drift by generation 50.
source: Even in the unrealistic situation of complete selfing during the experiment, and considering effective population sizes on the order of 1000 (Chelo and Teotónio, 2013), less than 5% was expected to be lost by genetic drift by generation 50, values that were not observed (only about half of the genetic variance was lost, Figure 7B).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with calculation and reference to figure.

claim: About half of the genetic variance was lost by generation 50.
source: Even in the unrealistic situation of complete selfing during the experiment, and considering effective population sizes on the order of 1000 (Chelo and Teotónio, 2013), less than 5% was expected to be lost by genetic drift by generation 50, values that were not observed (only about half of the genetic variance was lost, Figure 7B).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with reference to figure.

claim: Allelic diversity at neutral single-nucleotide polymorphisms is reduced relative to ancestral levels by 5% by generation 22.
source: Supporting loss of variation by selection we before showed that allelic diversity at neutral single-nucleotide polymorphisms is reduced relative to ancestral levels by 5% by generation 22 (Theologidis et al., 2014)
evidence: Stated in Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Allelic diversity at neutral single-nucleotide polymorphisms is reduced to 20% by generation 50.
source: and to 20% only by generation 50 (Chelo et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with citation.

claim: Variation in the ancestral g2,3 might have been lost by drift during the first 35 generations of the experiment.
source: Furthermore, our previous work suggests that variation in the ancestral g2,3 might have been lost by drift during the first 35 generations of the experiment such that they were perhaps of little consequence later on when populations reached the high salt environment (Guzella et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in Discussion with citation to previous work.

claim: Univariate and multivariate modeling approaches give similar results for estimating environmental effects.
source: We find that univariate and multivariate modeling approaches give similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 3, Figure 1—source data 4).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to figure supplement and source data.

claim: Estimates of phenotypic divergence are robust to multivariate and univariate modeling.
source: Estimates of phenotypic divergence are robust to multivariate and univariate modeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to figure supplement and source data.

claim: The ancestral G-matrix estimates are robust to changes in the prior distributions.
source: Our estimates are robust to changes in the prior distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to figure supplement showing sensitivity analysis.

claim: Selection differentials estimates are robust to variation in self-fertility.
source: These results are robust to variation in self-fertility (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to figure supplement showing sensitivity analysis.

claim: Traits with low genetic variance (FS and BS) do not appear to bias the genetic selection gradient estimates.
source: Traits with low genetic variance, FS and BS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), do not appear to bias the genetic selection gradient estimates (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to figure supplements.

claim: An alternative eigentensor analysis to detect genetic divergence among the 4 populations confirms the random skewers analysis.
source: An alternative eigentensor analysis to detect genetic divergence among the 4 populations confirms the random skewers analysis (see results in our GitHub appendix).
evidence: Stated in Results with reference to supplementary analysis.
